PetroSA

By: Joy Summers | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Profligacy, corruption, greed and billions lost at Petrosa, and yet Minister Mantashe refuses to reveal multibillion rand diesel contracts. Petrosa is nothing more than an expensive middleman surround

Unique Selling Point:
An investigation with new information and new voices into the parastatal. A story that clearly contradicts the Presidents anti corruption drive, as his own minister admits that secrecy at Petrosa is here to stay.

Summary:
SECRET DIESEL DEALS
Not long before Andre De Ruyter left Eskom, he complained that ESKOM couldn’t get a license to buy diesel directly from traders, to run the open cycle gas turbines that were keeping the lights on, when the country’s power stations were choking and breaking on bad coal. Instead PETROSA was importing the diesel he needed, and charging a premium to Eskom whose balance sheet threatened the economic stability of the country. But mining minister Gwede Mantashe dug in his heels, PETRO SA was the only route for the diesel that De Ruyter needed. End of discussion, and so Eskom was forced to pay more, and so were we.

PETRO SA protested that they were not overcharging Eskom, but without that stream of income from the utility, PETROSA would have collapsed, because the very purpose of PETRO SA had been eroded by malfeasance and greed for over a decade. Where once it was called a beacon of hope for South Africa, by 2020, Petrosa was just a middleman selling diesel.

OILGATE, THE ANC AND DEATH OF A TYCOON
Petrosa started out in 2000 with a promising future, but only three years later the company was mired in scandal, when R11 million of a R14 million deal was found to have been siphoned off to fund the 2004 ANC election campaign. The man at the center of that deal, tycoon Sandy Majali later revealed in a letter the ANC had in fact benefited to the tune of R18 million rand, and he threatened to reveal all in 2010. But a few weeks later he was dead, his body found in a Sandton hotel the day after Christmas.

But Oilgate was just the beginning. PETROSA executives fueled by their own importance went on a massive expansion drive. Always with the promise of benefits to the state, but the riches never found their way into government coffers and most of the deals ended up as losses. In 2010, Petrosa spent R16 million on the World Cup and justified it as a relations building exercise. They swanned off to Equatorial Guinea and Egypt where they invested R2 billion in exploration, later the company was forced to write down those investments to zero.

By 2015, Petrosa had spent R14 billion rand looking for new sources of gas. Drilling was done incorrectly, horizontally instead of vertically we are told. Minister Dipuo Peters brought in a new board and asked them to sort out the mess.

“ We kept asking them where is the gas, and when is it coming online” says a former board member who now questions the purpose of Petrosa. But the gas never came, and eventually the plug was pulled on the project. No gas but R14 billion down the tubes.

Many of the board members who tried to clean up the company, left when President Zuma replaced minister Dipuo Peters with Ben Martins as the energy minister. They could see that that further political meddling would be the order of the day. They weren’t wrong. In 2018 Petrosa was about to sign an ambitious R22 billion risky commitment to Nigerian oilfields owned by the Jacob Zuma foundation benefactor Kase Lawal. The new minister of energy, Jeff Radebe stepped in and stopped the deal.


Further information:
MOUNTING LOSSES
From 2005 to 2021 Petrosa lost R41 billion, and R4 billion in irregular expenditure, with a paltry R300 million contributed to SARS. We know that the local community don’t benefit, and if the fiscus keeps losing, what really is the point, except to make a few executives fabulously wealthy?

“Nothing makes sense” says Liz McDaid. “It’s the same as the nuclear deal. It doesn’t matter if nothing gets completed, but along the way there are millions to be made in management fees, and contracts, and then in ten years from now its’s all written down to zero again. Just like Project Ikhwezi. R14 billion with nothing to show for it. McDaid is also working with her team to track down the executives who have left Petrosa and are now working in private companies that stand to benefit when Petrosa gets new investment and starts up again.

THE MORE THINGS CHANGE...
By 2021, the gas in the Southern Ocean had run out and without gas, Mossgas came to a standstill and there was nothing for the workers to do on the rig 100 kms out in the Indian Ocean. But the workers go anyway and do little to nothing for two weeks at a time.
“ Well the managers need to be able to “manage” says local activist Bongani Swartbooi. If there are no workers, how do they justify their management?

THE MERGER THAT NEVER HAPPENED.
In March 2021, parliament was told that PETROSA was going to merge with Igas and the strategic fuel fund, and a new company called the South African national Petroleum company would emerge. Minister Mantashe told parliament the merger was of the utmost importance because it had the objective of setting up a formidable sustainable petroleum company for the country. The deadline was April 2021. But 2024 is around the corner, Mossgas is falling apart, the rig is apparently dangerous, and talks of any merger seemed to have disappeared.

ROTTING FROM THE HEAD
Meanwhile the current chair of Petrosa, Nkululeko Poya is in the spotlight. His dodgy past as the CEO of the railway regulator has caught up with him. Kevin Mileham, part of the oversight committee and DA MP has demanded his suspension for creating a fraudulent court order which he submitted to Petrosa to facilitate his appointment as the CEO.
“ I knew as soon as I saw that court order it was a fake” says the former board member. Nevertheless Poya remains in his position, and recently defended the latest Petrosa scandal to hit the headlines, Project Mthombo.

PROJECT MTHOMBO
Petrosa led the project which promised a multibillion rand oil refinery that was to be built at the Coega Economic Zone in Gqeberha. “R200 million has been spent on feasibility studies and legal advisory” according to Poya. The refinery was expected to create 27 000 temporary and 18500 permanent jobs. But once again the project has cost millions, made a few people rich and gone nowhere.


NOTHING BUT AN EXPENSIVE MIDDLEMAN
Poya also told City press that Petrosa plan was to continue increasing imported finished products that are supplied to the market within the country. That has left two former board members scratching their heads. “How can you import diesel when your very purpose is to be making the diesel!’ asked one of them, and then burst out laughing.

R3 BILLION RAND LOOKING FOR A MANAGEMENT COMPANY
And the deadline of 2024 to decommission the wells is almost upon Petrosa. They need R13 billion for that liability but there is only R3billion in the kitty. Now inexplicably they have put out the management of this R3 billion to tender. How does that even make sense.

DRILLING SOON TO BEGIN
Another deal that doesn’t make sense is Total energies drilling that is supposed to begin soon in blocks 9 and 11 off the Southern Coast. They have just completed their EIA up and down the coast, but they can’t tell anyone who they are selling the gas to. It only makes sense says Liz McDaid, if you understand that Shell has 40% of that deal and is still a benefactor for the ANC.

So that is where we are now. In 2023, after losing billions, Petrosa and Minister Mantashe are still operating in secret. When questioned about the secrecy around the current diesel contracts the minister brushed off Carte Blanche and AmaBhungane’s questions. They will remain secret, according to Mantashe, even if there are allegations that commodity traders are paying bribes of R3million rand per shipment to named executives of PETROSA and CEF.

During our research Carte Blanche can reveal is that we know the names of at least two commodity traders bringing in diesel, Trafigura whose BEE partner is Mcebisi Jonas and Gunvor Petroleum.

Carte Blanche looks at the dirty deals, the profligacy, the billions in losses with no apparent benefit for the state, and questions how in 2023 when President Ramaphosa came into office on an anti-corruption ticket, secrecy at Petrosa can ever be tolerated.

Summary: SECRET DIESEL DEALS Not long before Andre De Ruyter left Eskom, he complained that ESKOM couldn’t get a license to buy diesel directly from traders, to run the open cycle gas turbines that were keeping the lights on, when the country’s power stations were choking and breaking on bad coal. Instead PETROSA was importing the diesel he needed, and charging a premium to Eskom whose balance sheet threatened the economic stability of the country. But mining minister Gwede Mantashe dug in his heels, PETRO SA was the only route for the diesel that De Ruyter needed. End of discussion, and so Eskom was forced to pay more, and so were we. PETRO SA protested that they were not overcharging Eskom, but without that stream of income from the utility, PETROSA would have collapsed, because the very purpose of PETRO SA had been eroded by malfeasance and greed for over a decade. Where once it was called a beacon of hope for South Africa, by 2020, Petrosa was just a middleman selling diesel. OILGATE, THE ANC AND DEATH OF A TYCOON Petrosa started out in 2000 with a promising future, but only three years later the company was mired in scandal, when R11 million of a R14 million deal was found to have been siphoned off to fund the 2004 ANC election campaign. The man at the center of that deal, tycoon Sandy Majali later revealed in a letter the ANC had in fact benefited to the tune of R18 million rand, and he threatened to reveal all in 2010. But a few weeks later he was dead, his body found in a Sandton hotel the day after Christmas. But Oilgate was just the beginning. PETROSA executives fueled by their own importance went on a massive expansion drive. Always with the promise of benefits to the state, but the riches never found their way into government coffers and most of the deals ended up as losses. In 2010, Petrosa spent R16 million on the World Cup and justified it as a relations building exercise. They swanned off to Equatorial Guinea and Egypt where they invested R2 billion in exploration, later the company was forced to write down those investments to zero. By 2015, Petrosa had spent R14 billion rand looking for new sources of gas. Drilling was done incorrectly, horizontally instead of vertically we are told. Minister Dipuo Peters brought in a new board and asked them to sort out the mess. “ We kept asking them where is the gas, and when is it coming online” says a former board member who now questions the purpose of Petrosa. But the gas never came, and eventually the plug was pulled on the project. No gas but R14 billion down the tubes. Many of the board members who tried to clean up the company, left when President Zuma replaced minister Dipuo Peters with Ben Martins as the energy minister. They could see that that further political meddling would be the order of the day. They weren’t wrong. In 2018 Petrosa was about to sign an ambitious R22 billion risky commitment to Nigerian oilfields owned by the Jacob Zuma foundation benefactor Kase Lawal. The new minister of energy, Jeff Radebe stepped in and stopped the deal. Further information: MOUNTING LOSSES From 2005 to 2021 Petrosa lost R41 billion, and R4 billion in irregular expenditure, with a paltry R300 million contributed to SARS. We know that the local community don’t benefit, and if the fiscus keeps losing, what really is the point, except to make a few executives fabulously wealthy? “Nothing makes sense” says Liz McDaid. “It’s the same as the nuclear deal. It doesn’t matter if nothing gets completed, but along the way there are millions to be made in management fees, and contracts, and then in ten years from now its’s all written down to zero again. Just like Project Ikhwezi. R14 billion with nothing to show for it. McDaid is also working with her team to track down the executives who have left Petrosa and are now working in private companies that stand to benefit when Petrosa gets new investment and starts up again. THE MORE THINGS CHANGE... By 2021, the gas in the Southern Ocean had run out and without gas, Mossgas came to a standstill and there was nothing for the workers to do on the rig 100 kms out in the Indian Ocean. But the workers go anyway and do little to nothing for two weeks at a time. “ Well the managers need to be able to “manage” says local activist Bongani Swartbooi. If there are no workers, how do they justify their management? THE MERGER THAT NEVER HAPPENED. In March 2021, parliament was told that PETROSA was going to merge with Igas and the strategic fuel fund, and a new company called the South African national Petroleum company would emerge. Minister Mantashe told parliament the merger was of the utmost importance because it had the objective of setting up a formidable sustainable petroleum company for the country. The deadline was April 2021. But 2024 is around the corner, Mossgas is falling apart, the rig is apparently dangerous, and talks of any merger seemed to have disappeared. ROTTING FROM THE HEAD Meanwhile the current chair of Petrosa, Nkululeko Poya is in the spotlight. His dodgy past as the CEO of the railway regulator has caught up with him. Kevin Mileham, part of the oversight committee and DA MP has demanded his suspension for creating a fraudulent court order which he submitted to Petrosa to facilitate his appointment as the CEO. “ I knew as soon as I saw that court order it was a fake” says the former board member. Nevertheless Poya remains in his position, and recently defended the latest Petrosa scandal to hit the headlines, Project Mthombo. PROJECT MTHOMBO Petrosa led the project which promised a multibillion rand oil refinery that was to be built at the Coega Economic Zone in Gqeberha. “R200 million has been spent on feasibility studies and legal advisory” according to Poya. The refinery was expected to create 27 000 temporary and 18500 permanent jobs. But once again the project has cost millions, made a few people rich and gone nowhere. NOTHING BUT AN EXPENSIVE MIDDLEMAN Poya also told City press that Petrosa plan was to continue increasing imported finished products that are supplied to the market within the country. That has left two former board members scratching their heads. “How can you import diesel when your very purpose is to be making the diesel!’ asked one of them, and then burst out laughing. R3 BILLION RAND LOOKING FOR A MANAGEMENT COMPANY And the deadline of 2024 to decommission the wells is almost upon Petrosa. They need R13 billion for that liability but there is only R3billion in the kitty. Now inexplicably they have put out the management of this R3 billion to tender. How does that even make sense. DRILLING SOON TO BEGIN Another deal that doesn’t make sense is Total energies drilling that is supposed to begin soon in blocks 9 and 11 off the Southern Coast. They have just completed their EIA up and down the coast, but they can’t tell anyone who they are selling the gas to. It only makes sense says Liz McDaid, if you understand that Shell has 40% of that deal and is still a benefactor for the ANC. So that is where we are now. In 2023, after losing billions, Petrosa and Minister Mantashe are still operating in secret. When questioned about the secrecy around the current diesel contracts the minister brushed off Carte Blanche and AmaBhungane’s questions. They will remain secret, according to Mantashe, even if there are allegations that commodity traders are paying bribes of R3million rand per shipment to named executives of PETROSA and CEF. During our research Carte Blanche can reveal is that we know the names of at least two commodity traders bringing in diesel, Trafigura whose BEE partner is Mcebisi Jonas and Gunvor Petroleum. Carte Blanche looks at the dirty deals, the profligacy, the billions in losses with no apparent benefit for the state, and questions how in 2023 when President Ramaphosa came into office on an anti-corruption ticket, secrecy at Petrosa can ever be tolerated. metadata.Summary: SECRET DIESEL DEALS Not long before Andre De Ruyter left Eskom, he complained that ESKOM couldn’t get a license to buy diesel directly from traders, to run the open cycle gas turbines that were keeping the lights on, when the country’s power stations were choking and breaking on bad coal. Instead PETROSA was importing the diesel he needed, and charging a premium to Eskom whose balance sheet threatened the economic stability of the country. But mining minister Gwede Mantashe dug in his heels, PETRO SA was the only route for the diesel that De Ruyter needed. End of discussion, and so Eskom was forced to pay more, and so were we. PETRO SA protested that they were not overcharging Eskom, but without that stream of income from the utility, PETROSA would have collapsed, because the very purpose of PETRO SA had been eroded by malfeasance and greed for over a decade. Where once it was called a beacon of hope for South Africa, by 2020, Petrosa was just a middleman selling diesel. OILGATE, THE ANC AND DEATH OF A TYCOON Petrosa started out in 2000 with a promising future, but only three years later the company was mired in scandal, when R11 million of a R14 million deal was found to have been siphoned off to fund the 2004 ANC election campaign. The man at the center of that deal, tycoon Sandy Majali later revealed in a letter the ANC had in fact benefited to the tune of R18 million rand, and he threatened to reveal all in 2010. But a few weeks later he was dead, his body found in a Sandton hotel the day after Christmas. But Oilgate was just the beginning. PETROSA executives fueled by their own importance went on a massive expansion drive. Always with the promise of benefits to the state, but the riches never found their way into government coffers and most of the deals ended up as losses. In 2010, Petrosa spent R16 million on the World Cup and justified it as a relations building exercise. They swanned off to Equatorial Guinea and Egypt where they invested R2 billion in exploration, later the company was forced to write down those investments to zero. By 2015, Petrosa had spent R14 billion rand looking for new sources of gas. Drilling was done incorrectly, horizontally instead of vertically we are told. Minister Dipuo Peters brought in a new board and asked them to sort out the mess. “ We kept asking them where is the gas, and when is it coming online” says a former board member who now questions the purpose of Petrosa. But the gas never came, and eventually the plug was pulled on the project. No gas but R14 billion down the tubes. Many of the board members who tried to clean up the company, left when President Zuma replaced minister Dipuo Peters with Ben Martins as the energy minister. They could see that that further political meddling would be the order of the day. They weren’t wrong. In 2018 Petrosa was about to sign an ambitious R22 billion risky commitment to Nigerian oilfields owned by the Jacob Zuma foundation benefactor Kase Lawal. The new minister of energy, Jeff Radebe stepped in and stopped the deal.
metadata.Further information: MOUNTING LOSSES From 2005 to 2021 Petrosa lost R41 billion, and R4 billion in irregular expenditure, with a paltry R300 million contributed to SARS. We know that the local community don’t benefit, and if the fiscus keeps losing, what really is the point, except to make a few executives fabulously wealthy? “Nothing makes sense” says Liz McDaid. “It’s the same as the nuclear deal. It doesn’t matter if nothing gets completed, but along the way there are millions to be made in management fees, and contracts, and then in ten years from now its’s all written down to zero again. Just like Project Ikhwezi. R14 billion with nothing to show for it. McDaid is also working with her team to track down the executives who have left Petrosa and are now working in private companies that stand to benefit when Petrosa gets new investment and starts up again. THE MORE THINGS CHANGE... By 2021, the gas in the Southern Ocean had run out and without gas, Mossgas came to a standstill and there was nothing for the workers to do on the rig 100 kms out in the Indian Ocean. But the workers go anyway and do little to nothing for two weeks at a time. “ Well the managers need to be able to “manage” says local activist Bongani Swartbooi. If there are no workers, how do they justify their management? THE MERGER THAT NEVER HAPPENED. In March 2021, parliament was told that PETROSA was going to merge with Igas and the strategic fuel fund, and a new company called the South African national Petroleum company would emerge. Minister Mantashe told parliament the merger was of the utmost importance because it had the objective of setting up a formidable sustainable petroleum company for the country. The deadline was April 2021. But 2024 is around the corner, Mossgas is falling apart, the rig is apparently dangerous, and talks of any merger seemed to have disappeared. ROTTING FROM THE HEAD Meanwhile the current chair of Petrosa, Nkululeko Poya is in the spotlight. His dodgy past as the CEO of the railway regulator has caught up with him. Kevin Mileham, part of the oversight committee and DA MP has demanded his suspension for creating a fraudulent court order which he submitted to Petrosa to facilitate his appointment as the CEO. “ I knew as soon as I saw that court order it was a fake” says the former board member. Nevertheless Poya remains in his position, and recently defended the latest Petrosa scandal to hit the headlines, Project Mthombo. PROJECT MTHOMBO Petrosa led the project which promised a multibillion rand oil refinery that was to be built at the Coega Economic Zone in Gqeberha. “R200 million has been spent on feasibility studies and legal advisory” according to Poya. The refinery was expected to create 27 000 temporary and 18500 permanent jobs. But once again the project has cost millions, made a few people rich and gone nowhere. NOTHING BUT AN EXPENSIVE MIDDLEMAN Poya also told City press that Petrosa plan was to continue increasing imported finished products that are supplied to the market within the country. That has left two former board members scratching their heads. “How can you import diesel when your very purpose is to be making the diesel!’ asked one of them, and then burst out laughing. R3 BILLION RAND LOOKING FOR A MANAGEMENT COMPANY And the deadline of 2024 to decommission the wells is almost upon Petrosa. They need R13 billion for that liability but there is only R3billion in the kitty. Now inexplicably they have put out the management of this R3 billion to tender. How does that even make sense. DRILLING SOON TO BEGIN Another deal that doesn’t make sense is Total energies drilling that is supposed to begin soon in blocks 9 and 11 off the Southern Coast. They have just completed their EIA up and down the coast, but they can’t tell anyone who they are selling the gas to. It only makes sense says Liz McDaid, if you understand that Shell has 40% of that deal and is still a benefactor for the ANC. So that is where we are now. In 2023, after losing billions, Petrosa and Minister Mantashe are still operating in secret. When questioned about the secrecy around the current diesel contracts the minister brushed off Carte Blanche and AmaBhungane’s questions. They will remain secret, according to Mantashe, even if there are allegations that commodity traders are paying bribes of R3million rand per shipment to named executives of PETROSA and CEF. During our research Carte Blanche can reveal is that we know the names of at least two commodity traders bringing in diesel, Trafigura whose BEE partner is Mcebisi Jonas and Gunvor Petroleum. Carte Blanche looks at the dirty deals, the profligacy, the billions in losses with no apparent benefit for the state, and questions how in 2023 when President Ramaphosa came into office on an anti-corruption ticket, secrecy at Petrosa can ever be tolerated.
